events.title: Rider Advocate brief: 7 claims (0 void)
events.body:
C1: The GPS track shows one off-route segment on this RydeTAXI trip: between 09:04 and 09:07 the driver covered 1.97 km where the optimal route covers 0.21 km, adding 1.76 km and straying up to 957 m from the optimal route, taking the trip to 11.7 km against an optimal 9.9 km (+1.8 km). [F1 F3] [RD-1]
C2: That segment is billed mileage on a metered RydeTAXI fare, so the 1.76 km extra entered the meter: the fare line shows excess distance billed of $2.55 at $1.41/km, on a total of $27.27 (distance $16.57 for 11.8 km). [F3 F4 F6] [RD-2]
C3: The rider never consented to the reroute: the complete, fully timestamped chat (2 messages) contains only the rider's 08:52 pickup message and the driver's 08:52 arrival message, and no route-change message or rider agreement appears anywhere before the 09:04 off-route segment started. [F3 F7 F8 F9] [RD-5]
C4: The driver's written statement that an accident on the Tampines Expressway made the detour unavoidable is a post-trip claim, and even on the traffic record it cannot exempt the segment under RD-4: the accident was reported at 08:44 and the Tampines Expressway speed band 1 record runs 08:46–09:04, both of which end at or before the 09:04–09:07 off-route segment, while the roads actually driven later (Punggol Road, Tampines Avenue 12) were flowing at band 4 (30–39 km/h), so no traffic record covers the replaced stretch at the time it was replaced. [F3 F10 F11 F12 F13 F14] [RD-4]
C5: Because the code-of-conduct-type exemptions do not apply, the unexempted segment is refundable mileage: 1.76 km × $1.41/km = $2.48 (rounded to the cent), which the rider requests be refunded as a voucher. [F3 F4] [RD-2 RD-1]
C6: The driver's 90-day record shows 4 disputes with 2 upheld, but no upheld route dispute, so the RD-6 repeat-offender flag for route deviation is not triggered on the record before the court. [F17] [RD-6]
C7: No message, statement or part of the complaint alleges a threat, harassment or dangerous driving, so the case does not require escalation under SAFE-1 or SAFE-2. [F7 F8 F10] [SAFE-1 SAFE-2]
Weaknesses: The traffic record does show a genuine incident: F14 logs an accident at 08:44 only 0 m from the optimal route with lanes blocked, and F11 shows the Tampines Expressway at speed band 1 (0–9 km/h) from 08:46, so the driver can argue under RD-4(a)/(b) that there was real congestion on the optimal route and a reasonable cause to leave it. | The off-route segment begins at 09:04, exactly when the band-1 record ends, so the driver can argue the congestion was still clearing and that the detour was the tail of a justified reroute — the rider's answer is that RD-4 requires the traffic evidence to cover the replaced stretch for the segment's own window, which F11 (ending 09:04) and F14 (reported 08:44) do not. | The refund on a metered RydeTAXI fare is limited to mileage units; F2's +5.4 min and F6's time charge $5.33 are not recoverable under RD-2, so the rider's recovery is small ($2.48) and the driver will stress that the trip was still completed at the estimate-plus-1.8 km. | The rider's own profile (F16) shows 2 disputes in 90 days, 0 upheld, which the driver may use to suggest the rider disputes fares habitually, though profile facts cannot decide the case. | F1/F3 rest on map-matching of a 957 m maximum deviation; a small part of the 1.76 km could be matching residual, and the driver may argue the segment was a single continuous manoeuvre rather than a route change.
Asks: refund_partial $2.48

claims.assertion: The GPS track shows one off-route segment on this RydeTAXI trip: between 09:04 and 09:07 the driver covered 1.97 km where the optimal route covers 0.21 km, adding 1.76 km and straying up to 957 m from the optimal route, taking the trip to 11.7 km against an optimal 9.9 km (+1.8 km).

That segment is billed mileage on a metered RydeTAXI fare, so the 1.76 km extra entered the meter: the fare line shows excess distance billed of $2.55 at $1.41/km, on a total of $27.27 (distance $16.57 for 11.8 km).

The rider never consented to the reroute: the complete, fully timestamped chat (2 messages) contains only the rider's 08:52 pickup message and the driver's 08:52 arrival message, and no route-change message or rider agreement appears anywhere before the 09:04 off-route segment started.

The driver's written statement that an accident on the Tampines Expressway made the detour unavoidable is a post-trip claim, and even on the traffic record it cannot exempt the segment under RD-4: the accident was reported at 08:44 and the Tampines Expressway speed band 1 record runs 08:46–09:04, both of which end at or before the 09:04–09:07 off-route segment, while the roads actually driven later (Punggol Road, Tampines Avenue 12) were flowing at band 4 (30–39 km/h), so no traffic record covers the replaced stretch at the time it was replaced.

Because the code-of-conduct-type exemptions do not apply, the unexempted segment is refundable mileage: 1.76 km × $1.41/km = $2.48 (rounded to the cent), which the rider requests be refunded as a voucher.
The driver's 90-day record shows 4 disputes with 2 upheld, but no upheld route dispute, so the RD-6 repeat-offender flag for route deviation is not triggered on the record before the court.
No message, statement or part of the complaint alleges a threat, harassment or dangerous driving, so the case does not require escalation under SAFE-1 or SAFE-2.

weaknesses: The traffic record does show a genuine incident: F14 logs an accident at 08:44 only 0 m from the optimal route with lanes blocked, and F11 shows the Tampines Expressway at speed band 1 (0–9 km/h) from 08:46, so the driver can argue under RD-4(a)/(b) that there was real congestion on the optimal route and a reasonable cause to leave it.

The off-route segment begins at 09:04, exactly when the band-1 record ends, so the driver can argue the congestion was still clearing and that the detour was the tail of a justified reroute — the rider's answer is that RD-4 requires the traffic evidence to cover the replaced stretch for the segment's own window, which F11 (ending 09:04) and F14 (reported 08:44) do not.

The refund on a metered RydeTAXI fare is limited to mileage units; F2's +5.4 min and F6's time charge $5.33 are not recoverable under RD-2, so the rider's recovery is small ($2.48) and the driver will stress that the trip was still completed at the estimate-plus-1.8 km.
The rider's own profile (F16) shows 2 disputes in 90 days, 0 upheld, which the driver may use to suggest the rider disputes fares habitually, though profile facts cannot decide the case.

F1/F3 rest on map-matching of a 957 m maximum deviation; a small part of the 1.76 km could be matching residual, and the driver may argue the segment was a single continuous manoeuvre rather than a route change.

[F7 F8 F9] [RD-3 RD-5 RD-4]
D6: This is a metered RydeTAXI trip (total charged $27.27 with distance $16.57 for 11.8 km and time $5.33 for 20.5 min, F6); the billed excess of 1.8 km converts to $2.55 at $1.41/km (F4), and that is the maximum exposure in this case — but since F3 is exempt, no part of it is refundable. [F4 F6] [RD-2]

The driver's written statement that an accident on the Tampines Expressway made the detour unavoidable is a post-trip claim, and even on the traffic record it cannot exempt the segment under RD-4: the accident was reported at 08:44 and the Tampines Expressway speed band 1 record runs 08:46–09:04, both of which end at or before the 09:04–09:07 off-route segment, while the roads actually driven later (Punggol Road, Tampines Avenue 12) were flowing at band 4 (30–39 km/h), so no traffic record covers the replaced stretch at the time it was replaced.

Because the code-of-conduct-type exemptions do not apply, the unexempted segment is refundable mileage: 1.76 km × $1.41/km = $2.48 (rounded to the cent), which the rider requests be refunded as a voucher.

The off-route segment begins at 09:04, exactly when the band-1 record ends, so the driver can argue the congestion was still clearing and that the detour was the tail of a justified reroute — the rider's answer is that RD-4 requires the traffic evidence to cover the replaced stretch for the segment's own window, which F11 (ending 09:04) and F14 (reported 08:44) do not.

The refund on a metered RydeTAXI fare is limited to mileage units; F2's +5.4 min and F6's time charge $5.33 are not recoverable under RD-2, so the rider's recovery is small ($2.48) and the driver will stress that the trip was still completed at the estimate-plus-1.8 km.

The incident report at 08:44 (F14) pre-dates the start of the off-route segment at 09:04 (F3), so the corroborating traffic fact covers the substituted portion of the optimal route and the segment qualifies for exemption under RD-4(a).

Independent congestion data confirms the incident was still affecting the optimal route during the trip window: TAMPINES EXPRESSWAY recorded speed band 1 (0–9 km/h) from 08:46–09:04 (F11), a severe-congestion reading on the very road named in the accident report, corroborating the need to divert rather than continue on the optimal route.

The rider's own 90-day profile shows 2 disputes with 0 upheld (F16), which supports treating this complaint as unsupported rather than as a pattern of genuine overcharging.

weaknesses: F1 and F2 show the trip ran 11.7 km vs 9.9 km optimal (+18%) and 20.5 min vs 15 min (+5.4 min), which on its face supports the rider's 'longer than estimate' complaint; I can only answer it with the RD-4(a) exemption, not by denying the extra distance.

F3 shows the off-route segment went as far as 957 m off the optimal route, so the rider may argue the diversion was not the minimal workaround the incident required — I have no fact showing the diversion length was necessary.

F11's severe-congestion band on the Tampines Expressway ends at 09:04, exactly when the off-route segment begins (F3), so the rider can argue the congestion had cleared and the diversion was no longer justified at the moment it started; the accident report F14 is my only surviving corroboration.

The driver's explanation for the reroute appears only in his post-trip written statement (F10), not in the in-app chat (F9), which the rider will use to argue the justification was constructed after the fact.

The fare bill (F6) includes a $1.47 platform fee and a metered time component of $5.33 for 20.5 min; if the judge declines the RD-4 exemption, RD-2's extra-km formula (F4: $2.55) would produce a partial refund against us.

points.response: Conceded that F14 documents a real accident 0 m from the optimal route and that the Tampines Expressway is the road being avoided — but presence of an incident is not enough; RD-4 requires the corroboration to target the replaced stretch for the segment's own window, which F14/F11 do not.

A report time of 08:44 is not a coverage window: the only Tampines Expressway speed record ends at 09:04 (F11), exactly when the off-route segment begins (F3), so no traffic fact covers the replaced stretch during 09:04–09:07.

F11 is a band-1 record but its window 08:46–09:04 closes before the diversion; and under RD-4(b) a speed band, even a severe one, is corroboration only and cannot exempt a segment on its own, least of all one outside its time window.
The RD-4 exemption fails for want of time-window coverage, so the segment is an unexempted off-route segment under RD-1 and RD-2 yields 1.76 km × $1.41/km = $2.48, not $0.

Agreed that RD-5 consent is not in issue, but that cuts against the driver: with no passenger request in the chat (F7, F8, F9), the diversion stands or falls on RD-4 alone, and RD-4 does not reach it.

The maximum exposure on a metered ride is indeed the mileage unit billed, and the driver's own figure of $2.55 (1.8 km × $1.41/km, F4) confirms the extra distance entered the meter; the rider claims only the 1.76 km of the single off-route segment (F3), $2.48.
Headed nowhere: the rider does not seek an account flag, as C6 already stated the RD-6 predicate is not met on F17.

F16 is a profile fact with 0 upheld disputes against the rider and is barred from deciding anything under RD-6; it also cannot erase a GPS-recorded 1.76 km off-route segment (F3) that the traffic record does not cover.

Conceded that F3 records one off-route segment (09:04–09:07, +1.76 km, up to 957 m off route) and that trip distance was 11.7 km against 9.9 km optimal (F1); what C1 omits is that the deviation is only a violation if unexempted, and F14 exempts it.

Conceded that this is a metered RydeTAXI fare and that the extra distance entered the meter (distance $16.57 for 11.8 km, excess 1.8 km = $2.55 at $1.41/km, total $27.27, F4/F6); the mileage amount is refundable only if the segment is unexempted under RD-2, and F14 makes it exempt, so the formula returns $0 here.

Accepted as stated: the complete timestamped chat (F7, F8, F9) contains no route request or agreement, so RD-5 consent is absent — but RD-5 is not our route to exemption; RD-4 is, and RD-4 needs no rider consent, only a reasonable cause documented by traffic facts.

F14 satisfies RD-4(a) in terms: the Accident on the Tampines Expressway towards Tampines Mall was reported 08:44 at 0 m from the optimal route with lanes blocked — it therefore concerns the very stretch that was replaced, and its report time pre-dates the segment start of 09:04, which is the timing test RD-4(a) actually applies; F11's band-1 reading (0–9 km/h, 08:46–09:04) independently confirms that stretch was still severely congested in the trip window, and F12/F13's band-4 speeds merely show the alternative roads the driver used were better than the blocked expressway.

Since F14 exempts the segment under RD-4(a), it is not an unexempted segment and RD-2 yields no refund — and note the rider's own arithmetic (1.76 km × $1.41 = $2.48) conflicts with the fare fact F4, which bills the excess at $2.55 for 1.8 km, so the claimed figure is not computable from the fare record as submitted.
Agreed, and it is also our own point D7: with route disputes upheld at 0 in the 90-day profile (F17), the RD-6 repeated-violation predicate is not met, so no flag_account attaches in this case.
Agreed: nothing in the chat (F7, F8), the driver's statement (F10) or the complaint alleges any threat, harassment or dangerous driving, so no SAFE-1/SAFE-2 escalation arises.

The fare stands as charged, so there is no refund and no Ryde voucher on this trip. Nothing changes on your account.
